{{Short description|Ring of circles between two tangent circles}}
[[File:Pappus Chain Full.svg|thumb|A Pappus chain]]

In [[geometry]], the '''Pappus chain''' is a ring of [[circle]]s between two [[tangent circles]] investigated by [[Pappus of Alexandria]] in the 3rd century [[AD]].

==Construction==

Given two circles {{mvar|C{{sub|U}}}} and {{mvar|C{{sub|V}}}}, let the inner circle {{mvar|C{{sub|U}}}} be enclosed by the outer circle {{mvar|C{{sub|V}}}}, and let the two circles be tangent to each other at point {{mvar|A}}. Let the radii of these two circles be denoted as {{mvar|r{{sub|U}}, r{{sub|V}}}}, respectively, and let their respective centers be the points {{mvar|U, V}}.  The Pappus chain consists of the circles in the shaded grey region, which are externally tangent to {{mvar|C{{sub|U}}}} (the inner circle) and internally tangent to {{mvar|C{{sub|V}}}} (the outer circle).  Let the radius, diameter and center point of the {{mvar|n}}<sup>th</sup> circle of the Pappus chain be denoted as {{mvar|r<sub>n</sub>, d{{sub|n}}, P{{sub|n}}}}, respectively.

The Pappus chain is often considered with respect to an [[arbelos]], a [[circular triangle]] whose three sides are semicircles of the two given tangent circles and of the circle in the chain whose center is collinear with the two given circles.

==Properties==
===Centers of the circles===
====Ellipse====
All the centers of the circles in the Pappus chain are located on a common [[ellipse]], for the following reason.  The sum of the distances from the {{mvar|n}}<sup>th</sup> circle of the Pappus chain to the two centers {{mvar|U, V}} of the arbelos circles equals a constant

<math display=block>
\overline{P_nU} + \overline{P_nV} = 
(r_U + r_n) + (r_V - r_n) = r_U + r_V </math>

Thus, the [[Focus (geometry)|foci]] of this ellipse are {{mvar|U, V}}, the centers of the two circles that define the arbelos; these points correspond to the midpoints of the line segments {{mvar|{{overline|AB}}, {{overline|AC}}}}, respectively.

====Coordinates====
If <math>r = \tfrac{\overline{AC}}{\overline{AB}},</math> then the center of the {{mvar|n}}th circle in the chain is:

<math display=block>(x_n,y_n) = \left(\frac{r(1+r)}{2[n^2(1-r)^2+r]}~,~\frac {nr(1-r)}{n^2(1-r)^2+r}\right)</math>

===Radii of the circles===
If <math>r = \tfrac{\overline{AC}}{\overline{AB}},</math> then the radius of the {{mvar|n}}th circle in the chain is:
<math display=block>r_n = \frac {(1-r)r}{2[n^2(1-r)^2 + r]}</math>

===Circle inversion===
[[File:Pappus Chain Theorem.svg|thumb|right|250px|Under a particular inversion centered on {{mvar|A}}, the four initial circles of the Pappus chain are transformed into a stack of four equally sized circles, sandwiched between two parallel lines.  This accounts for the height formula {{math|1=''h{{sub|n}}'' = ''nd{{sub|n}}''}} and the fact that the original points of tangency lie on a common circle.]]
The height {{mvar|h{{sub|n}}}} of the center of the {{mvar|n}}<sup>th</sup> circle above the base diameter {{mvar|ACB}} equals {{mvar|n}} times {{mvar|d{{sub|n}}}}.<ref>Ogilvy, pp. 54&ndash;55.</ref>  This may be shown by [[Circle inversion|inverting in a circle]] centered on the tangent point {{mvar|A}}.  The circle of inversion is chosen to intersect the {{mvar|n}}<sup>th</sup> circle perpendicularly, so that the {{mvar|n}}<sup>th</sup> circle is transformed into itself.  The two arbelos circles, {{mvar|C{{sub|U}}}} and {{mvar|C{{sub|V}}}}, are transformed into parallel lines tangent to and sandwiching the  {{mvar|n}}<sup>th</sup> circle; hence, the other circles of the Pappus chain are transformed into similarly sandwiched circles of the same diameter. The initial circle {{math|''C''<sub>0</sub>}} and the final circle {{mvar|C{{sub|n}}}} each contribute {{math|{{sfrac|2}}''d{{sub|n}}''}} to the height {{mvar|h{{sub|n}}}}, whereas the circles {{math|''C''<sub>1</sub>}} to {{math|''C''<sub>''n''&minus;1</sub>}} each contribute {{mvar|d{{sub|n}}}}.  Adding these contributions together yields the equation {{math|1=''h{{sub|n}}'' = ''nd<sub>n</sub>''}}.

The same inversion can be used to show that the points where the circles of the Pappus chain are tangent to one another lie on a common circle.  As noted above, the [[Inversive geometry|inversion]] centered at point {{mvar|A}} transforms the arbelos circles {{mvar|C{{sub|U}}, C{{sub|V}}}} into two parallel lines, and the circles of the Pappus chain into a stack of equally sized circles sandwiched between the two parallel lines.  Hence, the points of tangency between the transformed circles lie on a line midway between the two parallel lines.  Undoing the inversion in the circle, this line of tangent points is transformed back into a circle.

===Steiner chain===
In these properties of having centers on an ellipse and tangencies on a circle, the Pappus chain is analogous to the [[Steiner chain]], in which finitely many circles are tangent to two circles.
